question:
Patient note:
A 64-year-old man is reviewed this morning in the day-surgery holding area before an outpatient arthroscopic debridement and partial medial meniscectomy of the right knee that the orthopedic team anticipates will last less than one hour under general anesthesia with regional block for post-operative analgesia. He reports that mechanical knee pain has curtailed his weekend pickle-ball games over the past four months, but he continues to walk his dog two miles each evening and perform light yardwork, climbing a flight of stairs at home without dyspnea or assistance. He has not been hospitalized, undergone any operative or endoscopic procedures, or worn splints, casts, or braces in the current calendar year, and the last time he entered an operating room was seven years ago for an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy. Pulmonary history is notable for tobacco-related chronic obstructive lung disease diagnosed in his early fifties after a 35-pack-year exposure; he quit cigarettes nine years ago and now uses once-daily tiotropium in combination with as-needed albuterol, has never required home oxygen, and has avoided oral steroids for more than eighteen months. He denies winter hospital admissions, mechanical ventilation, or nebulizer dependence. Cardiovascular review is benign for orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, or recent episodes of sudden weight gain, and a transthoracic echocardiogram performed during hypertension work-up last summer documented a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 60 % with normal valves. He denies chest pain, exertional angina, palpitations, syncope, and there is no history of coronary intervention or myocardial infarction. He has never experienced unilateral calf tenderness, asymmetric leg girth, unexplained shortness of breath, or hemoptysis, and prior imaging of the lower extremities and chest has never demonstrated venous or pulmonary clot. Lifelong bowel habits are regular, he has never been told he has Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis, and colonoscopy three years ago was normal aside from two small hyperplastic polyps. A review of the electronic chart confirms no malignancies, no cerebrovascular events, no spinal injuries, and no fractures of the hip, pelvis, or long bones. Regarding thrombosis risk, the patient recalls that his older sister spent a week in the intensive-care unit with a “blood clot in the lungs” after elective gynecologic surgery in her forties and that his father received anticoagulation for proximal leg thrombosis following a long trans-Atlantic flight; prompted by that pedigree, his primary physician ordered a hypercoagulability panel five years ago which was negative for common genetic mutations but did reveal mildly elevated fasting plasma homocysteine, for which he now takes daily folic acid and vitamin B12. He does not take estrogenic or selective estrogen receptor–modulating drugs, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or chronic systemic glucocorticoids. Current outpatient medications include tiotropium 18 µg inhaled every morning, albuterol 90 µg two puffs as needed, lisinopril 20 mg once daily for blood-pressure control, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, over-the-counter folic acid 1 mg, cyanocobalamin 1,000 µg, and a multivitamin; he discontinued low-dose aspirin one week ago per anesthesia instructions. He drinks one or two beers on weekends, denies illicit drug use, and has remained abstinent from nicotine since quitting. Physical examination finds an alert, well-nourished man sitting comfortably with a body mass index of 27 kg/m². Vital signs obtained ten minutes ago show temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg, pulse 82 beats per minute regular, respiratory rate 15 per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air. Neck veins are not distended, carotid upstrokes are brisk, and heart sounds are normal without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs are clear except for faint end-expiratory wheezes over the right mid-lung but no crackles. The abdomen is soft and nontender with active bowel sounds. Inspection of both lower limbs reveals no dilated superficial veins, no edema, and equal calf circumferences; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ bilaterally, and Homan-like maneuver elicits no discomfort. The right knee exhibits a small joint effusion, crepitus on flexion past 90 °, and medial joint-line tenderness, while the contralateral knee is unremarkable. Skin integrity is intact throughout and there are no active ulcers or hematomas. Neurologic screening shows full orientation, symmetrical strength, and intact sensation distally. A single 20-gauge peripheral intravenous catheter placed in the left antecubital fossa runs lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate; no tunneled lines, ports, or peripherally inserted central catheters are present. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn at 0600 reveal hemoglobin 14.3 g/dL, hematocrit 43 %, platelets 235 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 7.1 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, creatinine 0.95 mg/dL, AST 24 U/L, ALT 22 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.0 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A portable chest radiograph reviewed by radiology this morning shows mild hyperinflation consistent with his chronic lung disease but otherwise clear fields and normal cardiac silhouette; spirometry from clinic last month recorded an FEV₁ of 78 % predicted without significant bronchodilator response. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram displays normal sinus rhythm at 80 beats/min with nonspecific T-wave flattening in the inferior leads unchanged from prior tracings. Airway assessment reveals Mallampati class II, full cervical extension, and intact dentition, suggesting straightforward intubation. Sequential pneumatic compression sleeves have been placed around both calves but remain disengaged while final consents are signed, and no anticoagulant has yet been administered pending discussion with anesthesia and surgery regarding neuraxial block timing.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini VTE score adds weighted perioperative risk factors:
- Age 61–74: age 64 → 2.
- BMI >25 kg/m²: BMI 27 → 1.
- Abnormal pulmonary function: established COPD → 1.
- Arthroscopic surgery: planned knee arthroscopy → 2. Do not also count it as minor surgery.
- Family history of VTE: sister had PE and father had DVT → 3, counted once.
- Elevated plasma homocysteine: previously documented → 3.
He remains ambulatory, has no personal VTE history, and has only a peripheral IV. No other documented factor adds points. Sum = 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 12.
Final answer: 12
